key: And it came to pass after these things, that God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: ‘Abraham’; and he said: ‘Here am I.’
s: With Isaac born and Ishmael sent away, the chapter turns to God’s command to offer Isaac up; Ramban, on 22:1, reads the trial as for Abraham’s good, a command bringing his readiness from potential into deed, to reward the act and not the intent alone.

evidence.gloss: (Ramban on 22:1, ‘God did prove Abraham’) The matter of the trial, in my view, is this: because a man’s deeds are wholly in his own power, to do or not to do as he wills, it is called a ‘trial’ from the side of the one tried; but the One who tries, blessed be He, commands him so as to bring the thing out from potential into act, that he may have the reward of a good deed and not the reward of a good heart alone … And so all the trials in the Torah are for the good of the one tried.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Genesis 22:1, at [21,1]). Opened packet.js tanakh 6 --verse 22:1 and read Ramban’s whole comment on the verse: the trial is so called from the side of the one tried, because his deeds are in his own free power; from God’s side it is a command to bring the thing from potential into act, so that he has the reward of a good deed and not of a good heart alone; God tries the righteous whom He knows will obey, and all the Torah’s trials are for the good of the one tried. The sentence carries exactly this; ‘readiness’ and ‘intent’ gloss הדבר and לב טוב without drift. Plain sense faithful: Isaac is born (21:1 to 21:7) and Ishmael sent away (21:14) earlier in the day, and chapter 22 turns to the command to offer Isaac (22:2); no run of the key verse repeated. Evidence recopied from the packet and re-found by recheck-evidence’s matcher. Entry unchanged; entry-check ok.
